title: Choosing a fraud threshold
objective: Learners see that moving a fraud model’s decision threshold trades false alarms against missed fraud, and read the trade-off as a confusion matrix, precision and recall.

recommended.why: A custom D3 view puts every transaction on the score line next to a live confusion matrix, so learners see exactly which cases flip when the threshold moves.

alternative.why: A custom combined view versus standard curves: which shows the trade-off better?

assumptions: Synthetic data: 400 transactions with scores from a made-up fraud model, drawn with a fixed seed
Fraud and legitimate scores overlap, as they do for real models, so no threshold is perfect
A transaction is flagged when its score is at or above the threshold
Changing the fraud rate keeps 400 transactions and swaps legitimate ones for fraud ones
checkDescription: The four counts add up to all 400 transactions, precision equals TP/(TP+FP) and recall equals TP/(TP+FN) at the current threshold, and recall never rises as the threshold goes up.

learnerPrompts.predict: If you raise the threshold from 0.50 to 0.70, what happens to the number of false alarms, and to the number of missed frauds?
learnerPrompts.explain: At a 2 % fraud rate, precision drops sharply even though recall barely changes. Why do rare events make false alarms dominate the flags?
